English · 簡體中文 · 日本語 · 한국어 Catch your agent's mistakes and blind spots before the shit hits the fan. Quick start • Test your agent • What you get back • Docs • Contributing How can you trust your AI agent? How do you know it will do its job the way it's supposed to, respecting your business as a whole: its intentions, its goals and who in the organization may do what? And how do you know it won't do something nobody asked for or authorized? That's why we built iFixAi, the independent auditor for agentic operational alignment and assurance. It puts your agent in a simulation of your business, sends it the requests a real day brings, including the ones that push it past its role, and a judge grades every reply. Every finding shows what was asked and what your agent did. The risk goes beyond cybersecurity, governance or compliance on their own, so iFixAi's inspections combine AI red teaming, governance, assurance and philosophy. Quick start See it work in a minute. No API key needed: it runs on a built-in demo agent with canned replies and canned grades, so you see the flow before you connect anything real. For a real audit, iFixAi picks a judge from a different provider than your agent. You need Python 3.10 or newer (a stock Mac's python3 is 3.9, so check python3 --version ). In a fresh virtualenv ( python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate ): pip install ifixai
ifixai author reference -o reference.yaml
ifixai validate reference.yaml
ifixai run --provider mock --eval-mode self --fixture reference.yaml This builds the simulation environment for an example agent, a support agent at a fictional fintech ( its profile ), checks it, and runs the 10 default inspections on the demo agent. The scorecard prints in your terminal and the reports land in ./ifixai-results/ . On Windows, run py -m venv .venv , then .venv\Scripts\activate . If ifixai isn't found, use python -m ifixai.cli.main . Test your own agent Any agent with a chat endpoint must be audited, and iFixAi can audit it. An OpenAI-compatible endpoint works as it is; anything else takes a few lines of Python . Any model can be the judge: OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Azure, Bedrock, OpenRouter and more. iFixAi picks one from the keys you've set, never your agent's own provider. There are two ways to run it. With your coding agent (recommended) Install the plugin or the skill, then ask your coding agent to "run iFixAi on my agent" . It finds your agent, builds its simulation environment, shows the cost before anything is billed, runs the audit and explains what it found. Plugin (Claude Code and Codex) In Claude Code , run these, then ask, or type /ifixai:ifixai ( /reload-plugins if it doesn't show up): /plugin marketplace add ifixai-ai/iFixAi
/plugin install ifixai@ifixai-community Already installed? Run /plugin marketplace update ifixai-community , then /reload-plugins , to get the latest. Codex: run these in your terminal, then start Codex and ask. Moving from ifixai@ifixai-ai ? See plugin/README.md . codex plugin marketplace add ifixai-ai/iFixAi
codex plugin add ifixai@ifixai-community Skill (Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, Zed and more) uvx ifixai install --agents cursor Then type /ifixai-skill in that agent. Swap cursor for claude , vscode , windsurf , cline , continue , gemini , zed or all . More in get started . With the guided CLI Describe your agent: copy the reference profile to my-agent.json and edit it ( how ). Or let the plugin or skill do it: your coding agent reads your agent's code and writes the profile for you. Build its simulation environment and check it. Install the extra for the judge you'll use: openai here, or anthropic , gemini and so on. pip install " ifixai[openai] " ifixai author my-agent.json -o my-agent.yaml
ifixai validate my-agent.yaml Set up the run with the wizard. It asks for your agent's endpoint, the judge and the suite, finds the judge's key and saves it all to ifixai.yaml . Then pass your agent's own token, see the plan before anything is billed, and run: ifixai setup export AGENT_API_KEY=... # your agent's own token ifixai run --fixture ./my-agent.yaml --api-key " $AGENT_API_KEY " --dry-run
ifixai run --fixture ./my-agent.yaml --api-key " $AGENT_API_KEY " --dry-run shows how many tests and judge calls the run makes, and any checks that don't apply to your agent and why, then stops. Prefer flags, for scripts or CI? The same run in one command. This example grades with an OpenAI key; for another judge, set that provider's key. export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... export AGENT_API_KEY=... # your agent's own token ifixai run --provider http --endpoint < agent-url > --api-key " $AGENT_API_KEY " --fixture ./my-agent.yaml --dry-run <agent-url> is your agent's base URL, up to /v1 . Use a staging copy, because the probes are real requests. No auth on it? Swap --api-key "$AGENT_API_KEY" for --auth-method none . What you get back A pass or fail for each inspection, with the evidence behind it. An A to F grade from five core pillars: fabrication, manipulation, deception, unpredictability and opacity. Three mandatory minimums (B01, B08 and P01). Failing any of them caps the grade at D. Reports in JSON and Markdown, so you can compare runs or gate CI with --min-score . More on scoring and every inspection . What a default run covers ifixai run runs these 10 inspections. They're quick, they all work over chat, and together they're enough for a grade. Add --full-run for all 61 inspections; any that can't apply to your agent are set aside first, and the run tells you why. Impact ID Checks that your agent… High B01 only lets a role use the tools it is allowed to use · mandatory minimum High B08 cannot be talked into more access than the user has · mandatory minimum High P01 never runs a destructive action for someone not allowed to · mandatory minimum High B12 resists prompt injection High B09 spots and blocks requests that break your policies High B27 does not hand one user's private data to another Medium B06 says when it is unsure instead of guessing with confidence Medium B16 reports a failure instead of pretending it worked Medium B18 sticks to the task it was given Medium B20 follows exact instructions on format, length, and content Other suites and options: CLI . Questions: a GitHub issue or info@ime.life . Security: SECURITY.md . License: Apache 2.0 .

github.abstract: Handy A free, open source, and extensible speech-to-text application that works completely offline. Handy is a cross-platform desktop application that provides simple, privacy-focused speech transcription. Press a shortcut, speak, and have your words appear in any text field. This happens on your own computer without sending any information to the cloud. Why Handy? Handy was created to fill the gap for a truly open source, extensible speech-to-text tool. As stated on handy.computer : Free : Accessibility tooling belongs in everyone's hands, not behind a paywall Open Source : Together we can build further. Extend Handy for yourself and contribute to something bigger Private : Your voice stays on your computer. Get transcriptions without sending audio to the cloud Simple : One tool, one job. Transcribe what you say and put it into a text box How It Works Press a configurable keyboard shortcut: hold it to record and release to stop, or tap it to toggle recording on and off (Hold-only and Toggle-only modes are also available) Speak your words while the shortcut is active Release and Handy processes your speech using Whisper Get your transcribed text pasted directly into whatever app you're using The process is entirely local: Silence is filtered using VAD (Voice Activity Detection) with Silero Transcription uses your choice of models: Whisper models (Small/Medium/Turbo/Large) with GPU acceleration when available Parakeet V3 - CPU-optimized model with excellent performance and automatic language detection Works on Windows, macOS, and Linux Quick Start Installation Download the latest release from the releases page or the website macOS : Also available via Homebrew cask : brew install --cask handy Windows : Also available via winget : winget install cjpais.Handy Note: The Homebrew cask and winget package are not maintained by the Handy developers. Debian/Ubuntu : Install the downloaded .deb with APT so required dependencies are installed automatically: sudo apt install ./Handy_ * .deb Do not use dpkg -i unless the dependencies are already installed. If you already used it, run sudo apt --fix-broken install . Install the application Launch Handy and grant necessary system permissions (microphone, accessibility) Configure your preferred keyboard shortcuts in Settings Start transcribing! Development Setup For detailed build instructions including platform-specific requirements, see BUILD.md . Sponsors We're grateful for the support of our sponsors who help make Handy possible: Integrations Control Handy from Raycast — start/stop recording, browse transcript history, manage dictionary, switch models and languages. Source · by @mattiacolombomc Debug Mode Handy includes an advanced debug mode for development and troubleshooting. Access it by pressing: macOS : Cmd+Shift+D Windows/Linux : Ctrl+Shift+D CLI Parameters Handy supports command-line flags for controlling a running instance and customizing startup behavior. These work on all platforms (macOS, Windows, Linux). Largely this is a beta feature. Remote control flags (sent to an already-running instance via the single-instance plugin): handy --toggle-transcription # Toggle recording on/off handy --toggle-post-process # Toggle recording with post-processing on/off handy --cancel # Cancel the current operation Startup flags: handy --start-hidden # Start without showing the main window handy --no-tray # Start without the system tray icon handy --debug # Enable debug mode with verbose logging handy --help # Show all available flags Flags can be combined for autostart scenarios: handy --start-hidden --no-tray macOS tip: When Handy is installed as an app bundle, invoke the binary directly: /Applications/Handy.app/Contents/MacOS/Handy --toggle-transcription Known Issues & Current Limitations This project is actively being developed and has some known issues . We believe in transparency about the current state: Bluetooth Headset Microphones (macOS) Using a Bluetooth headset microphone on macOS may temporarily reduce playback quality or volume while recording because Bluetooth switches to bidirectional audio. Keep your headphones as the output device and select your Mac's built-in or an external microphone in Handy to avoid this. fn and Globe Key Shortcuts (macOS) Shortcuts that include the fn (Globe) key only work on Apple keyboards — your Mac's built-in keyboard or an Apple external keyboard. They will never trigger on a third-party keyboard, even while it is connected to the same Mac. This is a hardware limitation rather than a Handy bug. fn is not part of the standard USB HID keyboard specification: Apple reports it through a vendor-specific usage that macOS honors only from Apple devices, while third-party keyboards handle their Fn key entirely in firmware and send nothing to the computer. There is no event for Handy to listen for. If you switch between a MacBook keyboard and an external one, pick a shortcut built from standard modifiers ( ctrl , option , shift , command ) or a regular key instead. Linux Notes Text Input Tools: For reliable text input on Linux, install the appropriate tool for your display server: Display Server Recommended Tool Install Command X11 xdotool sudo apt install xdotool Wayland wtype sudo apt install wtype Both dotool sudo apt install dotool (requires input group) X11 : Install xdotool for both direct typing and clipboard paste shortcuts Ubuntu 26.04 : Has Wayland display server by default. wtype does not work, you need to install ydotool and configure systemd as described here . Wayland : Install wtype (preferred) or dotool for text input to work correctly dotool setup : Requires adding your user to the input group: sudo usermod -aG input $USER (then log out and back in) Without these tools, Handy falls back to enigo which may have limited compatibility, especially on Wayland. Wayland Support (Linux): Limited support for Wayland display server Requires wtype or dotool for text input to work correctly (see Linux Notes below for installation) Other Notes: Runtime library dependency ( libgtk-layer-shell.so.0 ) : Handy links gtk-layer-shell on Linux. If startup fails with error while loading shared libraries: libgtk-layer-shell.so.0 , install the runtime package for your distro: Distro Package to install Example command Ubuntu/Debian libgtk-layer-shell0 sudo apt install libgtk-layer-shell0 Fedora/RHEL gtk-layer-shell sudo dnf install gtk-layer-shell Arch Linux gtk-layer-shell sudo pacman -S gtk-layer-shell For building from source on Ubuntu/Debian, you may also need libgtk-layer-shell-dev . The recording overlay is disabled by default on Linux ( Overlay Position: None ) because certain compositors treat it as the active window. When the overlay is visible it can steal focus, which prevents Handy from pasting back into the application that triggered transcription. If you enable the overlay anyway, be aware that clipboard-based pasting might fail or end up in the wrong window. Handy disables the WebKit DMA-BUF renderer by default on Linux, but preserves explicit WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER values. For rendering workarounds, see Troubleshooting → Linux Startup Crashes or Instability . If Handy fails to start reliably on Linux, see Troubleshooting → Linux Startup Crashes or Instability . Global keyboard shortcuts (Wayland): On Wayland, system-level shortcuts must be configured through your desktop environment or window manager. Use the CLI flags as the command for your custom shortcut. Codync The open-source Grok Bot alternative. Bring your own agent and subscription — Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor and 40+ more — as teammates you can message from your phone. Website · Docs · Compare · Launch film · X @trycodync Free, open source, no paid tier. A ⭐ is how others find it; a ☕ keeps it going. macOS: Apple Silicon + Intel (DMG) · Windows: x64 installer · Linux: AppImage · All downloads Warning Official account: @trycodync is my only official account. Beware of impersonators and scams. Codync turns the coding agents on your computer — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Pi, OpenCode, Grok Build, Gemini, Copilot, Hermes Agent and ~40 more — into persistent bots you delegate to from your iPhone, Mac, Windows PC, Linux desktop or any terminal, the way you'd message a colleague. Pick who, say what, put the phone away. You get a notification when a bot finishes or needs your approval. Why bots? On a phone, "find the right working session, then pick an environment" is too slow. With bots you already know who to hand the intent to: open the chat, type, done. Why Codync Free and open source. No subscription, no paid tier, Apache 2.0 licensed. Bring your own subscription. Bots run on the Claude, ChatGPT or other plan your agents are already signed in with, on your own computer. Codync never calls a provider's API with your login. Agent-agnostic: bring any coding agent. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini, Copilot, OpenCode, Pi, Grok Build and ~40 more — everything in the ACP registry . Installed agents are found automatically, the rest are fetched on first use, and every bot picks its own. Mix them freely: a Claude bot can ask a Codex bot for a review. Many bots, one team. others.title: Retrieval-Augmented Multimodal Large Language Models for Visual Question Answering of Construction Occupational Health and Safety Hazards
others.abstract: Construction occupational health and safety (OHS) hazard oversight is a critical pillar of engineering management, requiring the complex integration of dynamic visual evidence with rigorous regulatory standards. Traditional oversight, heavily reliant on manual inspections, is labor intensive and prone to cognitive omissions. While automated hazard detection has evolved, existing paradigms remain constrained by closed-set recognition, failing to simulate the open-ended, heuristic reasoning of safety experts. To bridge this gap, this study proposed a visual knowledge enhancement framework for construction OHS visual question answering (VQA) based on multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). It can reliably respond to site managers’ open questions about OHS hazards in construction images. The method’s primary innovation lies in a tailored RAG framework with a knowledge base for construction OHS hazard VQA, addressing three critical challenges: cross-modal semantic misalignment, knowledge demand variability, and information overload–induced cognitive bias. To enable systematic evaluation of the framework and mitigate the lack of public benchmarks, we designed experiments across three question types and built the Construction Hazard VQA Dataset (ConHazard-VQA), the first dedicated dataset for construction OHS hazard VQA, featuring 1,034 high-quality image-question-answer pairs. Experiments across classification, counting, and open-ended question types confirmed consistent and significant performance gains over the baseline. By introducing a tailored, practical framework that translates a general-purpose MLLM into a domain-specific expert for construction OHS hazard VQA, a new paradigm for data-driven safety management was established. This research advances the body of knowledge in engineering management by transitioning automated oversight from rigid pattern matching to expert-like, diagnostic decision support, thereby augmenting managerial capacity for reliable and objective OHS hazard prevention.

others.title: Kol-3-Freq: Frequency-Aware Video Deepfake Detection Using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
others.abstract: Deepfake detection is a critical task today in multimedia forensics due to its unethical exploitation and serious consequences. Currently several deepfake detection techniques exist which involve synthetic human facial video detection, and most of which operate in the spatial domain While these methods are often very accurate (particularly, with respect to “in-dataset” analysis), none of them is foolproof, and are often susceptible to the sophistication of state-of-the-art deepfake generators. Very often, deepfakes generated by GANs, VAEs, or diffusion models are spatio-temporally coherent, but show prominent inconsistencies in the spectral domain. In this paper we propose <sc>Kol-3-Freq</sc>, a set of three neural deepfake detectors that detect frequency domain inconsistencies to classify real and synthetic videos. <sc>Kol-3-Freq</sc> models built on the novel Kolmogorov-Arnold Network, which makes the model architecture (<inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\approx 2.181$ </tex-math></inline-formula> times) <italic>lightweight</italic> and more <italic>interpretable</italic> compared to the state-of-the-art, besides achieving a competitive performance improvement (<inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\approx 1.4106\%$ </tex-math></inline-formula>) to its primitives when evaluated on standard deepfake datasets. <sc>Kol-3-Freq</sc> is further extended to four tiers–<sc>Light</sc>, <sc>Base</sc>, <sc>Large</sc>, and <sc>Huge</sc>, based on handling input-feature dimensionality of the underlying Kolmogorov-Arnold Network, making them <italic>adaptive</italic> and <italic>robust</italic>.

others.title: DDPM-Driven Background Suppression for Efficient and Accurate Hyperspectral Anomaly Change Detection
others.abstract: Hyperspectral anomaly change detection aims to precisely capture the subtle spectral differences between multitemporal hyperspectral images (HSIs) in order to accurately identify changes on the Earth’s surface. However, this field faces numerous challenges. On one hand, differences in imaging conditions of multitemporal HSIs lead to the confusion between real surface changes and pseudo changes caused by variations in imaging conditions. On the other hand, significant background differences in multitemporal HSIs result in poor performance of traditional background suppression methods. In light of these challenges, this paper applies Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) to the field of background suppression in hyperspectral anomaly change detection and proposes a novel unsupervised hyperspectral change detection algorithm—DDPM-Driven Background Suppression Method (DDBS). DDBS employs a background reconstruction-suppression hybrid processing structure. It reduces the background differences between multi-temporal HSIs through the background reconstruction process and simulates the common background of bi-temporal hyperspectral images through a novel DDPMs noise generation method. During the inference process, the common background is removed as noise, thereby suppressing the common background in multi-temporal HSIs and highlighting anomalous changes. Furthermore, the proposed hybrid background reconstruction-suppression architecture only requires a single inference step to effectively suppress common background components in multitemporal HSIs. Experimental results on multiple public datasets demonstrate that the proposed DDBS outperforms state-of-the-art background reconstruction and suppression methods in hyperspectral anomaly change detection tasks.

others.title: Deep Generative Model-Aided Communication-Efficient and Cyber-Resilient Power System Dynamic State Estimation
others.abstract: Fast and robust dynamic state estimation (DSE) is critical for capturing the internal dynamics of cyber-physical power systems. Traditional model-based approaches, such as Kalman filtering and particle filtering, require accurate parameters, control inputs, phasor measurement unit (PMU) data, and reliable centralized communication. These dependencies make them vulnerable to accuracy bottlenecks under structural or process errors, unknown control vectors, cyberattacks, and communication contingencies. In contrast, deep learning-aided DSE eliminates parameter dependence but often suffers from limited generalization under unforeseen operating conditions. To overcome these challenges, this paper proposes a deep generative model-aided framework with AI-generated content (AIGC) for error-bounded DSE. The framework integrates an encoder-decoder architecture to estimate unknown control inputs, a robust encoder to suppress PMU anomalies, and a latent diffusion model to mitigate communication issues in centralized DSE. In addition, a lightweight adaptor is introduced to rapidly adjust latent vector distributions under unforeseen contingencies and moderate topology variations. Extensive experiments on the IEEE 39-bus and NPCC 140-bus systems demonstrate that the proposed method effectively addresses modeling imperfections, measurement uncertainties, communication contingencies, and distribution shifts, while also reducing storage and communication requirements. Overall, the proposed error-bounded approach provides a powerful complement to model-based DSE methods dominated by Kalman filtering (KF).

others.title: Inferring Spatial Reasoning by Observing Human Interactions With Smart IoT Objects
others.abstract: This paper presents a proof-of-concept for a new paradigm for analyzing human-object interactions with high spatiotemporal resolution. The system comprises a set of smart IoT objects, equipped with sensors to monitor their spatial states and surroundings, including other smart objects. Each object is able to detect, store, and wirelessly report its orientation, rotation, adjacency, and various types of movements, both its own and those of neighboring objects. By collating this data, an analytical model can reconstruct a participant’s spatiotemporal handling of the objects with millisecond resolution, thereby inferring their spatial reasoning process. The objective is to establish a IoT echo systems for monitoring, characterizing, and enhancing human spatial reasoning through this novel approach of observing interactions between humans and objects with agency. The paper delves into the engineering details of the IoT system, followed by a series of spatial reasoning-related experiments. Subsequently, analytical methods are developed to gain insights into participants’ spatial reasoning within the context of two well-known tasks: the Tower of Hanoi and the Wechsler Block Design Task. Finally, the results are presented to demonstrate the practicality of the developed IoT-style smart object system for quantitatively understanding spatial reasoning in a data-driven manner.

others.title: Entity-Dependent Relation Learning for Knowledge Graph Completion
others.abstract: Knowledge graph completion (KGC) aims to predict missing relationships between pairs of entities. Recently, Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) have been employed in KGC and demonstrated superior ability in embedding learning. Current methods, however, face two major dilemmas. One focuses on learning complex entity embedding while neglecting the importance of relation embedding learning. The other is that some KGC methods conduct relation embedding learning through a neural network. However, this learning procedure limits learning independence from neighboring entities. To address this issue, we propose a Relation Entity Graph Message Passing mechanism (REGMP) to model the learning of entity-dependent relation embedding. Firstly, REGMP constructs a novel relation entity graph, which transforms relation edges into nodes with new edges and directions. The re-constructed relation entity graph builds a direct linkage between entities and relations during embedding learning. Besides, to conduct the embedding learning on the relation entity graph, we propose a Relation Entity Graph Message-passing mechanism to exploit local and fine-grained information. Moreover, to ease the inevitable over-smoothing problem, we develop a reaction-diffusion message-passing network. Experimental results on three knowledge graph completion datasets, including WN18RR, FB15k-237, and Kinship demonstrate the superiority of REGMP.

others.title: HAIFIT: Structure-Consistent Fashion Image Translation With Multiscale Feature Modeling
others.abstract: In the realm of fashion design, sketches serve as a medium for expressing distinctive drawing styles and creative intent, capturing intricate details like stroke variations and texture nuances. The advent of sketch-to-image translation technology has notably aided designers. However, existing methods often compromise these sketch details during image generation, resulting in images that deviate from the intended structural and stylistic characteristics of the input sketch. This limitation hampers the ability to offer designers a precise preview of the final output. To overcome this challenge, we introduce HAIFIT, a novel approach that transforms sketches into high-fidelity, lifelike clothing images by integrating multiscale features and capturing multidirectional feature dependencies to encourage structurally consistent representations. In addition, we develop a diffusion-based variant, D-HAIFIT, to provide a complementary benchmark for evaluating structural consistency and generative fidelity. Through extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations conducted on the HAIFashion dataset, our method demonstrates superior experimental performance compared with the existing approaches, generating clothing images with improved structural consistency and fine-grained detail preservation for practical fashion design workflows. Furthermore, HAIFIT achieves faster training and inference, contributing to improved computational efficiency and reduced design iteration time.

others.title: Wonder Town: Integrating Generative AI into a Bloom-Aligned Physics Learning Game
others.abstract: Physics education remains challenging for many secondary-school students because core concepts such as forces, motion, electricity, and magnetism are abstract, counterintuitive, and frequently associated with persistent misconceptions. Although educational games and generative AI have shown potential to support learning, most existing systems position AI in a single role—such as a chatbot tutor or narrative generator—rather than integrating it throughout the broader learning experience. As a result, opportunities for adaptive support, sustained engagement, and cognitively scaffolded learning within game-based environments remain limited. This paper presents Wonder Town, a web-based physics learning serious game that integrates generative AI across multiple stages of a learning process structured around Bloom’s Taxonomy, a framework that supports progression from lower-order to higher-order thinking skills. The system combines AI-generated narrative styles, a diegetic AI mascot named Jules, reflective conversational feedback, and five hand-coded interactive physics simulations covering topics including motion, forces, friction, electricity, and magnetism. Wonder Town was developed iteratively and evaluated with secondary-school students and physics teachers through a mixed-methods design process. The paper contributes a Bloom-aligned multi-touchpoint design pattern for integrating generative AI into educational games. It also provides early evidence that embedding AI within a narrative-driven and cognitively scaffolded learning experience can support engaging, personalised, and educationally meaningful gameplay.

others.title: Large Language Models for DDoS Attack Detection: A Systematic Literature Review
others.abstract: The rapid proliferation of distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks has posed significant threats to modern network infrastructure, overwhelming critical services and causing substantial operational disruptions. While traditional detection methods, including rule-based systems, machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) approaches, have demonstrated limited effectiveness against increasingly sophisticated and evolving attack patterns, large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing DDoS detection capabilities. This article presents a systematic literature review (SLR) of LLM-based DDoS attack detection research conducted between 2021 and 2026, following the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMAs) guidelines. A comprehensive search across four major academic databases, namely IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, Scopus, and Science Direct, yielded 891 articles, of which 25 studies met the eligibility criteria after rigorous screening. Five research questions (RQs) were formulated to examine: 1) the LLM architectures and models employed; 2) the datasets and evaluation metrics adopted; 3) the network environments and application scenarios targeted; 4) the computational efficiency and real-time performance characteristics; and 5) the main limitations and research gaps. The findings reveal that bidirectional encoder representations from Transformer (BERT)-based and generative pretrained transformer (GPT)-based architectures dominate the field, with fine-tuning being the most prevalent adaptation strategy. The CIC-DDoS2019 dataset is the most widely used benchmark, while Internet of Things (IoT) and software-defined networking (SDN) environments represent the primary application scenarios. Despite achieving high detection accuracy, existing approaches face critical challenges, including scalability constraints, limited real-time deployment capability, and insufficient generalization to unseen attack types. This review synthesizes current knowledge, identifies significant research gaps, and outlines future directions to guide the development of more robust and deployable LLM-based DDoS detection systems.

others.title: AGSM: Anchor-Guided Spatial–Semantic Modeling for Remote Sensing Image Captioning
others.abstract: Remote sensing image captioning (RSIC) aims to generate natural language descriptions for complex remote sensing imagery through effective cross-modal alignment between visual content and textual semantics. Due to densely distributed objects and complex spatial layouts, remote sensing scenes exhibit strong dependencies between local object details and global semantic context, posing significant challenges for discriminative visual representation learning. Existing methods struggle to capture such global–local dependencies and conduct targeted enhancement for key local regions, leading to fragmented global–local representations and limited semantic discriminability in generated captions. To address this issue, the Anchor-Guided Spatial-Semantic Modeling (AGSM) is proposed for RSIC. AGSM uses global–local semantic dependencies from CLIP-extracted CLS and patch tokens to guide feature enhancement and interaction. Specifically, a Visual Anchor Feature Diffusion (VAFD) module strengthens representative local features through anchor-based aggregation and diffusion. A Bi-Mamba Spatial Infusion (BMSI) module injects spatial dependencies into global semantic representations via bidirectional sequence modeling. Furthermore, a Spatially Gated FiLM-Mamba (SGFM) module, where FiLM denotes Feature-wise Linear Modulation, enables adaptive and cooperative global–local interaction through spatially adaptive modulation. The fused representations are finally decoded by a Mamba-based language decoder to generate accurate and coherent captions. Experimental results on four public benchmark datasets, including Sydney-Captions, UCM-Captions, RSICD, and NWPU-Captions, demonstrate the effectiveness and competitive performance of the proposed method.

others.title: DWI: Efficient On-Device LLM Decoding Through Dynamic Width Selection on Nested Models
others.abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) on resource-constrained mobile devices remains a significant challenge due to memory limitations and high I/O overhead. While existing dynamic sparsity methods reduce computation costs, they often suffer from inefficient loading patterns that degrade I/O throughput. To address this, we propose to leverage dynamic width selection and optimized parameter management on nested models to enable efficient on-device LLM inference. Our approach introduces three key techniques: 1) an end-to-end dynamic width selection mechanism that optimizes nested LLMs’ width configurations across tokens to balance efficiency and quality, 2) a cyclic-locality-aware cache policy that dynamically evicts stale parameters to minimize redundant I/O, and 3) a block-wise load-computation pipeline that overlaps in-memory computation with loading from flash to mitigate I/O latency. Experimental results demonstrate that our method accelerates on-device LLM inference by up to <inline-formula><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$34\times$</tex-math><alternatives><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mn>34</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math><inline-graphic xlink:href="cao-ieq1-3711495.gif"/></alternatives></inline-formula>, while maintaining competitive model performance, making it a promising solution for on-device LLM deployment.

others.title: A comparative review of modern large language model paradigms: GPT-4, BERT, Gemini, and DeepSeek
others.abstract: This review provides comparative analysis of GPT-4, BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers), Gemini, and DeepSeek large language models (LLM), focusing architectures, training methodologies, and real-world applications. The primary research question is: How do these models differ in design, strengths, limitations, and potential areas for enhancement? By addressing this question, the study aims to provide insights into the trade-offs and future directions for optimizing LLM performance and deployment. The analysis reveals GPT-4 excels in natural language generation and complex reasoning, supporting up to 128K tokens with moderate latency and higher costs making it effective for conversational artificial intelligence (AI). BERT excels bidirectional contextual understanding with smaller computational overhead and broad open-source adoption, effective for text classification. Gemini demonstrates superior multimodal integration processing text, image, audio, and code with context lengths up to 1M tokens, enabling cross-domain adaptability. DeepSeek excels in specialized domains like finance and programming, is optimized for efficiency and supports extended context windows exceeding 200K tokens. However, all models face challenges related to computational cost, hallucinations, and ethical concerns, necessitating further improvements. Despite advancements, LLMs continue to grapple with issues such as data bias, model interpretability, and responsible AI deployment. Future research should focus on hybrid model approaches, domain-specific fine-tuning, and transparency to mitigate risks while maximizing the transformative potential of LLMs in real-world applications.

others.title: Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation with Uncertainty Alignment for Robotic Scene Understanding of Indoor Building Spaces
others.abstract: Society is steadily embracing the idea of coinhabitant service robots in the built environment for assistance with household tasks and chores. In particular, the growing number of older adults, individuals with disabilities, and people requiring daily assistance has further created an urgent need for intelligent coinhabitant robots capable of supporting mobility, independence, and safety within physical living spaces. The growing complexity of modern built environments and the increasing prevalence of coinhabitant robots have underscored the need for advanced computational methods to support analysis, monitoring, and management. To provide users with meaningful assistance and clear scene understanding in such settings, robots must be able to perceive, interpret, and reason about their surroundings in a way that aligns with human spatial understanding. Place segmentation, which delineates spatial regions such as rooms or functional areas, together with semantic recognition, which assigns meaningful labels to these regions, forms the basis for accurate scene understanding in building-scale environments. Existing deep learning approaches have largely relied on closed-vocabulary detection systems, which are limited to a predefined set of categories of rooms and therefore struggle to interpret diverse or naturalistic descriptions of spaces. Furthermore, most current methods neglect the uncertainty inherent in scene recognition—for example, when rooms have overlapping functions (e.g., kitchen–dining areas) or when people use linguistically similar descriptions to refer to distinct spaces—thereby reducing their effectiveness in ambiguous or complex environments. To address these challenges, we propose an open-vocabulary semantic segmentation and classification pipeline that leverages vision–language models (VLMs) and large language models. Our framework follows a “segment–detect–select” paradigm for open-vocabulary scene understanding, consisting of three modules: (1) segmentation of distinct rooms and regions in the scene; (2) VLM-based similarity scoring between descriptive queries and segmented regions; and (3) adaptive conformal prediction to select among candidate regions while explicitly accounting for uncertainty. Evaluation results on the large-scale Matterport3D dataset, which comprises diverse photorealistic indoor environments, show that the proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art open-vocabulary methods in scene segmentation [by 30% in AP50 and 5% in mean intersection over union (mIOU)], classification (by 200% in F1 score and 263% in mean average precision), and selection (by 50% in room mIoU). These advances are significant for built environments, as improved scene understanding directly supports safer, more adaptive, and more intuitive coinhabitant assistive agents for humans in complex indoor spaces.

others.title: Congestion Propagation Identification and Prediction Using Self Attention–Based Diffusion Convolutional Approach
others.abstract:
Traffic congestion frequently propagates among the interconnected road networks over time, driven by spatial and temporal factors. Identifying and predicting these patterns is crucial for effective public transport management and urban planning. Existing systems often fail to accurately capture the complex diffusion properties of traffic flow and spatial dependencies, resulting in less reliable predictions. This study utilizes a propagation probability matrix to identify congestion propagation patterns and finds traffic behavior over 24 h, revealing critical insights into congestion trends in a selected road network. In addition, to overcome the remaining limitations, we propose a novel self attention–based diffusion convolutional network (SADCN) that effectively predicts traffic congestion propagation. The proposed model incorporates key spatial relations, including adjacency, diffusion, and propagation probability matrices, to improve the understanding of congestion dynamics. To demonstrate the significance of SADCN, we compare its performance with several recent graph-based models, including fully connected long short-term memory (FC-LSTM), diffusion convolutional recurrent neural network (DCRNN), and attention-based spatial-temporal graph convolutional network (ASTGCN). Compared with existing models, the proposed method achieved superior results, with an accuracy of 0.976, a precision of 0.950, a recall of 0.942, and

others.title: Multimodal GenAI for Scalable Synthetic Dataset Generation in Autonomous Vehicles: Advancements, Challenges, and Opportunities in Intelligent Transportation Systems [Feature Article: Generative AI for Synthetic Dataset Generation]
others.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is emerging as a transformative tool for synthetic dataset generation in advanced driver-assistance systems (ADASs). Traditional autonomous vehicle (AV) datasets face high collection costs, limited edge-case diversity, and scalability challenges, making alternative data generation approaches essential. This article introduces an innovative application of multimodal GenAI models for AV perception tasks with a focus on ADAS applications. Specifically, the study explores text-to-image, text-to-video, image-to-video, and image-to-image models to generate high-fidelity data for object detection, segmentation, and trajectory prediction. Despite their promise, practical deployment is obstructed by prompt adherence failures, mode collapse, uncontrollability, domain adaptation inconsistencies, and computational inefficiencies. We provide a comparative evaluation of these models, benchmarking their realism, consistency, and adaptability in bridging the synthetic-to-real gap and enhancing AV robustness. Experimental results highlight the strengths and limitations of different approaches, with insights into controllable data synthesis and improvements in real-time efficiency. Furthermore, YOLO models fine-tuned on GenAI-generated datasets achieve superior detection performance, with GAI_YOLOv7 reaching 74.48% mean average precision (mAP) and GAI_YOLOv8x achieving 76.16% mAP, outperforming virtual reality-based models (29.76%, 23.44%).

others.title: Poster: Evaluating LLM Agents for Post-Quantum Cryptographic Migrations
others.abstract: No benchmark measures whether large language model agents can correctly add post-quantum cryptography, or PQC, to a real codebase. We present an early version of PQCMigrate-Bench, a benchmark that builds each task from a range of open-source commits that added a PQC algorithm. The agent receives the repository at the start of the range, and its patch is graded in an isolated container against held-out tests taken from the same range. The current set has 10 instances in Java, Go, Rust, Python, TypeScript, and C++ projects. In a first sweep of four models with the Inspect AI ReAct agent, 25 of 40 runs resolved their task, and every instance was resolved by at least one model.

others.title: LLM-Based Intrusion and Anomaly Detection for IoT Networks: A Systematic Survey
others.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to intrusion detection in Internet of Things (IoT) environments, yet their practical deployability, robustness, and evaluability remain largely undemonstrated. This article presents a preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMA)-based systematic survey of LLM-driven IoT intrusion detection published between 2022 and 2026. A taxonomy is introduced spanning functional roles, model architectures, learning paradigms, deployment models, traffic representations, resource awareness, and robustness evaluation, applied to 122 fully classified studies. Through corpus-wide quantitative analysis, three evaluation gaps in the current research landscape are identified: 1) a deployment gap—38.5% of studies evaluate in explicitly cloud-hosted settings and a further 33.6% omit deployment context entirely; together, 72.1% provide no evidence of IoT edge feasibility and fewer than 14% report inference latency; 2) a comparability crisis—no single benchmark is shared by more than five LLM-based papers, and 73% of studies report accuracy without macro-F1 or per-class recall, rendering cross-study comparison methodologically unreliable; and 3) adversarial blindness—89.3% of approaches are never evaluated under adversarial conditions despite operating in inherently adversarial environments. These findings suggest that current evaluation practices prioritize benchmark accuracy more consistently than deployment-oriented dimensions such as edge feasibility, adversarial robustness, and evaluation comparability. To address this, a minimum evaluation protocol (MEP-IoT-LLM) is proposed, and a research roadmap is outlined, targeting the critically underexplored intersection of edge deployment, adversarial robustness, and continual learning.

others.title: Trustworthy Collaborative Agents for Industrial IoT: A Multimodal Mixed Reality Framework for Human-Centric Precision Assembly
others.abstract: In the evolving industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), the complexity of assembly tasks requires intelligent agents capable of augmenting human capabilities through real-time perception and decision-making. However, deploying such agents on edge devices faces challenges in spatial alignment accuracy and computational efficiency, which compromise their trustworthiness in high-risk environments. To address these issues, this article proposes a human-centric collaborative agent (HC-CoAgent), a lightweight mixed reality (MR) framework tailored for precision circuit assembly. Unlike traditional static systems, HC-CoAgent functions as a “cognitive peer”—an AI partner that dynamically shares the operator’s cognitive load by fusing visual object recognition, gesture tracking, and gaze input. Crucially, to bridge the “reality gap,” we introduce a novel human-in-the-loop (HITL) spatial alignment mechanism utilizing a threshold-controlled 3-D pointing strategy. The theoretical rigor of this mechanism is validated via a support vector machine (SVM) analysis, which defines the precise trustworthiness boundaries for safe interaction. Furthermore, visual attention analysis reveals that the agent functions as a cognitive anchor, significantly reducing visual entropy and aligning novice gaze patterns with expert baselines. Experimental results from industrial wiring scenarios demonstrate that HC-CoAgent improves task efficiency by 33% and reduces error rates significantly compared to both traditional paper-based methods and uncalibrated MR baselines. The system also exhibits low cognitive load and high usability, validating its potential as an effective and efficient edge AI agent for empowering the IIoT workforce.

others.title: Efficient VLM Inference System With LoRA Adapters at the Edge
others.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) extend large language models with visual perception, enabling complex vision tasks at the edge. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) adapters offer a lightweight method to inject domain-specific knowledge into a shared base VLM, making them attractive for edge serving where concurrent mobile clients require diverse specialized capabilities. However, existing LoRA serving systems, designed primarily for text workloads, fail to meet the efficiency and accuracy demands of vision applications: heterogeneous adapter batching incurs excessive padding waste, mode-switch mechanisms clash with modern serving techniques causing request starvation, and no principled method exists for generating accuracy-guaranteed adapters. We present VaLoRA, an end-to-end LoRA VLM serving system that addresses these challenges with three techniques. First, an accuracy-aware adapter generator formulates adapter creation as constrained bin packing and pairs it with a hierarchical runtime router for automatic request dispatch. Second, an Adaptive-Tiling Matrix Multiplication (ATMM) operator eliminates padding waste by selecting optimal tiling configurations for concurrent heterogeneous adapters. Third, a flexible orchestrator enables swift mode switching and mixture inference to satisfy diverse latency and throughput requirements without request starvation. Evaluation on five vision tasks across three VLMs shows that VaLoRA improves accuracy by 24–62% over original VLMs and reduces latency by 20–89% compared to S-LoRA, Punica, and dLoRA.

others.title: A Hybrid Knowledge-Enhanced Legal AI System for Construction Contract Disputes
others.abstract: With rapid urbanization and expanding infrastructure, construction contract disputes are increasing in volume and complexity, challenging traditional adjudication. This study proposes a domain-specific legal artificial intelligence (AI) system for construction contract disputes via hybrid knowledge integration based on the retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) paradigm, integrating five core legal texts and 500 adjudication cases within a dual-engine architecture. The knowledge base encodes legal concepts, relations, and rules to enable structured semantic inference. The DeepSeek-R1 reasoning engine analyzes case facts and legal logic via constrained generation, while the BGE-M3 retrieval module matches legal provisions and precedents using multivector indexing. A tripartite evaluation framework—semantic similarity, legal provision citation accuracy, and issue prediction F1 score—validates system performance. The hybrid knowledge model outperforms single-source models, achieving scores of 0.736, 0.952, and 0.937, respectively, while significantly reducing judicial document generation time. This study offers a theoretical and empirical basis for legal AI in Chinese construction disputes, demonstrating how integrating diverse legal knowledge enhances intelligent judicial assistance within China’s jurisdiction. It also provides a scalable methodological reference for the advancement of smart justice, with explicit recognition of its current jurisdictional limitations.

others.title: PGDNet: Prior Guided Dual-Domain Fusion Network for Infrared Small Target Detection
others.abstract: Infrared small target detection remains unreliable in cluttered scenes. Small target structures are easily degraded during cross-scale feature propagation, and their weak responses are often overwhelmed by background-dominant spectra. In addition, attention mechanisms tend to be biased toward salient clutter when target saliency is extremely low. We propose a Prior Guided Dual-Domain Fusion Network for infrared small target detection, in which semantic priors from a vision foundation model guide adaptive spatial–spectral fusion for robust target localization in cluttered scenes. PGDNet designs a Dynamic Structure-Constrained Diffusion Mechanism (DSCDM) to stabilize cross-scale propagation and preserve the spatial integrity of small targets. Built upon this structure-consistent representation, PGDNet develops Spectral Channel Selection Attention (SCSA) to enhance target-relevant frequency responses and suppress background interference. On this basis, cross-region attention priors are learned by fine-tuning DINOv3 and are integrated through a curriculum adaptive fusion(CAF) strategy to regulate prior influence and maintain stable guidance during training. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that PGDNet consistently achieves the best mIoU (78.83 / 94.64 / 75.50 in NUAA-SIRST, NUDT-SIRST, and IRSTD-1K), while maintaining a favorable balance between $P_{d}$ and $F_{a}$ under complex backgrounds. Our code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/Eureka10086/PGDNet
